_meta.units: Years counted from the vintage unless a tier carries basis 'bottling' (years from bottling, for wines sold ready such as tawny Port, sherry and oxidative VDN) or 'disgorgement' (non-vintage sparkling).

fields.ready: years until the wine is approachable
fields.limit: outer limit for good examples stored well; most bottles fade before it

_meta.fine_units: Fine units (index fine: 1) resolve to a profile in this order: 1) _fine_profile[id]; 2) the unit's own id if profiled; 3) if the id contains '-premier-cru-' or '-grand-cru-', the profiled id before it (e.g. fr-givry-premier-cru-crausot -> fr-givry); 4) Italy only: the longest profiled id that prefixes the unit id followed by '-' (e.g. it-roero-valmezzana -> it-roero, it-etna-volpare -> it-etna), because Italian sub-unit ids are built from their appellation while their geometric parents can be wrong; 5) the first profiled id up the parent chain. Tier = _fine_override[id] if present in the profile, else the first candidate in _fine_tier['<profile id>|<subcat>'], else in _fine_tier['<country>|<subcat>'], that exists in the profile's tiers; else the profile's default_tier.
_meta.lookup: 1) profiles[appellation id]; fine units as in fine_units. 2) else _defaults['<country>|<style>|<category>'] (with '|<subcat>' for broad zones), then '<country>|<style>|*', '*|<style>|<category>', '*|<style>|*', '*|*|*'. Style is the index 'style' or the bottle's colour.
_meta.vintage_link: vintages.json windows are for the entry's ref tier; shift other tiers additively by the ready and limit differences.

fr-pauillac.why: Cabernet Sauvignon on deep, free-draining gravel gives small, thick-skinned berries and a lot of tannin, and the classed growths add new oak and long maceration on top. That tannin needs a decade or more to soften, while acidity from the Atlantic climate keeps the wines alive for decades beyond. Pauillac is the most tannic and long-lived of the communes.
fr-pauillac.producer_style: Traditional estates with long macerations and firm extraction need the longest; the riper, plusher style common since the late 1990s opens a few years sooner but rarely lasts longer. Second wines come from younger vines and are made to drink at five to fifteen years.

src.title: Conseil Interprofessionnel du Vin de Bordeaux
Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

fr-margaux.why: Cabernet Sauvignon on deep, free-draining gravel gives small, thick-skinned berries and a lot of tannin, and the classed growths add new oak and long maceration on top. That tannin needs a decade or more to soften, while acidity from the Atlantic climate keeps the wines alive for decades beyond. Margaux's thinner, sandier gravels give perfumed wines that usually open a little earlier than Pauillac.
fr-margaux.producer_style: Traditional estates with long macerations and firm extraction need the longest; the riper, plusher style common since the late 1990s opens a few years sooner but rarely lasts longer. Second wines come from younger vines and are made to drink at five to fifteen years.

fr-saint-emilion-grand-cru.producer_style: Traditional estates with long macerations and firm extraction need the longest; the riper, plusher style common since the late 1990s opens a few years sooner but rarely lasts longer. fr-meursault.why: Chardonnay on limestone keeps its acidity, and barrel fermentation and lees ageing add texture that evolves into nutty, honeyed complexity. Meursault and Puligny are the reference whites of the Côte de Beaune.
fr-meursault.producer_style: Since the mid-1990s many white Burgundies aged prematurely ('premox'), linked to reduced sulphur, softer pressing and certain corks; growers who adopted firmer pressing, more sulphur and better closures from about 2010 restored longevity. Lean, reductive styles age better than rich, lees-stirred ones.

fr-montrachet.why: Chardonnay on limestone keeps its acidity, and barrel fermentation and lees ageing add texture that evolves into nutty, honeyed complexity. Le Montrachet is the most concentrated white Burgundy and needs a decade.
fr-montrachet.producer_style: Since the mid-1990s many white Burgundies aged prematurely ('premox'), linked to reduced sulphur, softer pressing and certain corks; growers who adopted firmer pressing, more sulphur and better closures from about 2010 restored longevity. Lean, reductive styles age better than rich, lees-stirred ones.

fr-mercurey.why: Pinot Noir has thin skins and modest tannin, so its longevity comes from acidity and concentration rather than structure. On Côte d'Or limestone and marl, better sites give smaller yields and finer tannins, and the grand crus can develop for decades. The Côte Chalonnaise is cooler and later than the Côte d'Or and its reds are lighter.
fr-mercurey.producer_style: Whole-bunch fermentation and long, gentle extraction tend to give longer-lived wines with a closed phase around years three to eight; destemmed, early-picked modern styles are approachable sooner. Yield matters most: over-cropped wines fade fast whatever the label.

fr-chablis-grand-cru.producer_style: Old-barrel, low-yield producers make the longest-lived wines; Les Clos is the most structured.

fr-moulin-a-vent.producer_style: Traditional whole-bunch semi-carbonic wines are best early; destemmed, barrel-aged cuvées from old vines (Morgon Côte du Py, Moulin-à-Vent) age like Burgundy.

prestige.label: Prestige cuvée (Dom Pérignon, Krug, Cristal and peers)

fr-champagne.why: High acidity from a cool climate, autolysis on the lees and the protection of carbon dioxide let Champagne age far longer than most whites; it turns from citrus and brioche to toast, nuts and honey.
fr-champagne.producer_style: Houses that ferment or age reserve wines in oak, block malolactic or keep wines long on the lees make the longest-lived Champagnes; low-dosage, recently disgorged wines show their age sooner. Magnums age more slowly than bottles.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

fr-coteaux-champenois.why: Still Pinot Noir from Champagne's best villages: high acid, light body, surprising longevity.

fr-hermitage.why: Syrah on steep granite and schist keeps fresh acidity and builds firm, fine tannin; whole-cluster ferments and older oak add structure that needs years to resolve. Hermitage's south-facing granite hill gives the most powerful, longest-lived wines of the Rhône; the white Marsanne goes through a dumb phase from about year three to eight before turning honeyed and nutty.
fr-hermitage.producer_style: Traditional whole-bunch, large-cask producers (Chave, Clape, Jamet) make wines that close up for years and then last decades; destemmed, new-oak modern styles are plusher and open sooner.

fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.why: Grenache gives sweet fruit, high alcohol and modest tannin, so southern blends rely on Syrah and Mourvèdre for structure; the Mistral keeps the grapes healthy and concentrated. Châteauneuf's galets, sand and limestone give the south's most concentrated wines. Whites are lovely young, often close up, and re-emerge after about eight years.
fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.producer_style: Traditional estates using whole bunches, old foudres and a high share of Mourvèdre (Beaucastel) or old-vine Grenache (Rayas) make the longest-lived wines; super-ripe, new-oak 'prestige cuvées' are impressive young but can turn porty.

fr-jasnieres.why: Chenin Blanc has piercing natural acidity, so even dry Chenin on tuffeau and schist ages for decades, and the sweet wines, protected by sugar and acid, can last a century.
fr-jasnieres.producer_style: Producers who pick in several passes for botrytis or passerillage and ferment in old wood make the longest-lived wines; demi-sec often shuts down for years before opening.

fr-muscadet.why: Melon de Bourgogne is neutral and high in acidity; lees contact adds texture, and granite and gneiss sites give wines that age surprisingly well.
fr-muscadet.producer_style: Wines held on the lees for years before bottling age longest.

fr-alsace.why: Alsace's rain shadow behind the Vosges gives long, dry autumns; Riesling and Pinot Gris keep acidity and extract and age for decades, while Gewurztraminer's lower acidity makes it best younger.
fr-alsace.producer_style: Bone-dry, low-yield domaine wines (Trimbach, Zind-Humbrecht, Weinbach) last longest; residual sugar, which varies a lot, also helps preservation.

it-barolo.why: Nebbiolo combines very high tannin with high acidity and pale colour; the DOCG rules demand long ageing before release, and the tannin still needs years in bottle to soften into the tar-and-roses complexity it is famous for. Serralunga and Monforte give the firmest wines, La Morra and Barolo village the most perfumed.
it-barolo.producer_style: Traditional producers (long maceration of 30 to 60 days, large Slavonian botti: Bartolo Mascarello, Giacomo Conterno, Giuseppe Rinaldi) make wines that need a decade or more; modernists (short maceration, rotofermenters, French barriques) made wines that open five or so years sooner, and most estates now sit between the two.

it-brunello-di-montalcino.why: Sangiovese has high acidity and firm tannin but thin skins; on galestro and alberese limestone it makes cherry-and-earth wines that gain leather and tobacco notes over a decade or two. Montalcino's warmer, drier hill gives the most powerful Sangiovese; the northern slopes are fresher, the southern riper.
it-brunello-di-montalcino.producer_style: Traditional estates ageing in large Slavonian casks (Biondi-Santi, Soldera, Montevertine) make wines that need longer and last longer; the barrique-aged, often Merlot-boosted styles of the 1990s and 2000s open sooner.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

uga.label: Soave Classico from a named UGA

it-soave.why: Garganega on the volcanic basalt and limestone hills east of Verona; the hillside Classico zone and its 33 UGAs give wines with the acidity and extract to gain almond and honey notes over a decade.
it-soave.producer_style: Single-UGA bottlings from hillside growers (Pieropan, Inama, Gini, Suavia) age longest; plain Soave from the plain is for early drinking.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

rive.label: Prosecco Superiore Rive (single commune or hamlet)

it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.why: Glera from the steep hogback hills between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, made by the tank method for freshness; the 43 Rive and the Cartizze hill are the best-exposed slopes.
it-conegliano-valdobbiadene-prosecco.producer_style: Rive wines are vintage-dated and riper; Cartizze is usually off-dry. Sui lieviti (bottle-fermented, undisgorged) styles keep a little longer.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

it-valle-d-aosta.why: Alpine terraces along the Dora Baltea; cool nights keep acidity high, and the Nebbiolo of Donnas and Arnad-Montjovet is the only style built for long ageing.
it-valle-d-aosta.producer_style: Most wines are made for freshness; Donnas from traditional cellars needs several years.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

sottozona.label: Sottozona or Riserva (Predappio, Bertinoro, Modigliana and others)

it-romagna.why: Sangiovese on the Apennine foothills of Romagna; the named sottozone on sandstone and marl give fresher, more structured wines than the plain.
it-romagna.producer_style: Modigliana and Predappio growers making single-sottozona wines age them longest.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

it-gambellara.why: Garganega on volcanic hills next to Soave, made in a similar style.
it-gambellara.producer_style: Classico and named sottozone keep longer.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

it-val-d-arno-di-sopra.why: Upper Arno valley between Chianti and the Pratomagno ridge; an organic-only DOC whose Pietraviva and Pratomagno subzones grow Sangiovese and Bordeaux varieties.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

it-colli-di-conegliano.why: Hills around Conegliano; besides the reds, two rare passito sweet wines are protected as subzones.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

it-bagnoli-di-sopra.why: Raboso (Friularo) south of Padua: very high acidity and firm tannin that need years.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

it-lison.why: Tai (Friulano) on the Veneto-Friuli border: fresh, almond-scented whites.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

white_traditional.label: Traditional white Reserva or Gran Reserva

es-rioja.why: Tempranillo has moderate tannin and acidity; Rioja's long-standing practice of ageing in American and French oak before release means Reservas and Gran Reservas arrive already mature and hold a long plateau. The legal minimums are Crianza 2 years (1 in oak), Reserva 3 (1 in oak), Gran Reserva 5 (2 in oak).
es-rioja.producer_style: Traditional Haro houses (López de Heredia, La Rioja Alta, CVNE) release wines after long cask ageing and their Gran Reservas last half a century; modern 'vino de autor' styles with darker extraction and new French oak are built for 10 to 20 years.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

es-ribera-del-duero.why: Tinto Fino (Tempranillo) on the high Duero plateau, at 750 to 1,000 m, gets hot days and cold nights; thick skins give more colour and tannin than Rioja, so the wines need longer.
es-ribera-del-duero.producer_style: Vega Sicilia's Único spends a decade in wood and bottle before release and lasts for decades more; modern estates using new French oak make denser wines that open sooner.

src.title: Consejo Regulador DO Ribera del Duero
Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

es-toro.why: Tinta de Toro in a hot, dry climate gives powerful, tannic, high-alcohol wines.
es-toro.producer_style: Riper, oaky modern styles open sooner.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

top.label: Vi de finca, Gran Vinya Classificada, top estate

es-priorat.why: Old Garnacha and Cariñena on llicorella slate give tiny yields of concentrated, mineral wines with high acidity for their ripeness.
es-priorat.producer_style: Riper, oakier styles of the 1990s and 2000s gave way to fresher, earlier-picked wines that age at least as well.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

es-montsant.why: Priorat's neighbour on limestone and granite, fresher and earlier-drinking.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

es-jerez-xeres-sherry.producer_style: Look for the bottling date (lot number or back label): fino and manzanilla are best within a year; some producers argue en rama fino gains complexity for a few years.

es-manzanilla-sanlucar-de-barrameda.producer_style: Drink manzanilla fresh, ideally within months of bottling.

es-montilla-moriles.why: Sherry is fortified and aged in a solera, so it has no vintage and is ready when bottled. pt-porto.producer_style: Foot-trodden, lagar-fermented wines from old field-blend vineyards (Nacional, Vargellas Vinha Velha) age longest. LBV comes filtered (drink on release) or unfiltered (ages like a light Vintage Port).

pt-madeira.why: Madeira is heated and deliberately oxidised in cask, so nothing is left to spoil; with the island's high-acid grapes it is the longest-lived wine in the world.
pt-madeira.producer_style: Canteiro (cask) ageing in warm lofts makes the finest wines; estufa-heated wines are for early drinking. House and variety (Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malmsey, Terrantez) matter more than vintage.

de-mosel.why: Riesling's very high acidity, together with residual sugar in the Prädikat styles, preserves it for decades; slate and steep south-facing slopes ripen it slowly and give low alcohol and intense extract. The Mosel's slate slopes give the lightest, most delicate, longest-lived sweet Rieslings.
de-mosel.producer_style: Spontaneous fermentation in old Fuder casks and long lees ageing (Keller, Prüm, Egon Müller) give the longest-lived wines; young Riesling often shows sulphur and reductive notes that clear with a few years. Dry Grosses Gewächs goes through a closed phase around years three to six.

at-niederosterreich.why: Lower Austria spans the Danube regions; single-vineyard Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from primary rock and loess age for decades.
at-niederosterreich.producer_style: Estates that pick late and ferment in large old casks (Knoll, F.X. Pichler, Hirtzberger, Prager) make the longest-lived wines; botrytis-touched Smaragd ages faster.

at-burgenland.producer_style: Top single-vineyard Blaufränkisch needs a decade.

src.title: Oxford Companion to Wine, 5th ed. (Robinson and Harding, OUP 2023)

us-napa-valley.why: Napa's sunny, dry growing season ripens Cabernet fully every year, giving dense fruit and ripe, plentiful tannin; the best wines have the structure for decades, though their richness makes them enjoyable surprisingly young. The valley floor's alluvial benches (Oakville, Rutherford) give the classic dusty, plush Napa style.
us-napa-valley.producer_style: Riper, higher-alcohol, new-oak styles are seductive young and peak earlier; estates that pick earlier and use less new oak make wines that age more like their European models.
